::: {.why}
The single most used result in derivatives pricing, and given quadratic variation it is a two-line derivation rather than a mystery, which is why the last three days were spent on quadratic variation.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Derive Itô's lemma from a second-order Taylor expansion and say in words what the extra term is doing.
- Apply it to obtain the dynamics of the log of a geometric Brownian motion, and connect the result to volatility drag.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Derive it: expand a twice-differentiable function of a stochastic process to second order, substitute the quadratic variation identity for the squared increment, and drop the terms that vanish. Do it on paper without looking, then check against the notes.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Apply it to the log: with a process whose relative increments have constant drift and volatility, the log has drift reduced by half the variance. That result is exactly your day 31 arithmetic-geometric gap, arrived at from a completely different direction, and noticing that is worth more than either derivation alone.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [15 min]{.task-min} Verify by simulation: simulate the process and its log, and confirm the drift of the log matches the lemma's prediction to within sampling error.
:::
:::
